Manual Focus · Rider Panel

The Rider Panel: market research run on 500 AI cyclists living in the real UK

The Rider Panel is a simulated UK cycling market. Each of its 500 riders is an AI agent with a full life story, a home town and a budget. Many have friends in the panel too. They live through the run-up to Christmas in their town's real weather. They see real prices and the real competition. Give them a product and each one decides week by week whether to buy it. Then they tell you why.

It gives a brand or product manager an answer in an afternoon that used to take months of fieldwork.

What the Rider Panel is

What the Rider Panel is: 500 AI riders connected to the real world around them

Each rider is an AI agent. It isn't a persona on a slide or a survey answer. Each one carries a written life with a job and a home. Each has money worries or none, a partner who gets a say and a goal for the year. Then we connect every rider to the same forces that shape real buying decisions. Your product is the only thing that changes.

Their own lives

Home, job, money, family, kit and riding goals. The mix of riders follows UK survey data. Each rider then gets a written life story with something happening this winter. Most also have friends and club mates in the panel.

Why it matters

Why it matters: research that needed months and a big budget, now in an afternoon

Asking real customers is slow and expensive, so most brands only do it for their biggest launches. Everything else gets decided on instinct. The Rider Panel makes testing a launch cheap enough to do every time, before you spend money on stock and campaigns.

How a study works

How a study works, in four steps

  1. Set up the world

    Load this season's real weather for every rider's town. Add the calendar along with every rival product at its real price.

  2. Describe your launch

    Your product, price, retailers and reviews. Write each version you want to compare.

  3. Let the riders live it

    Every rider lives the season week by week and keeps a diary. They decide whether to buy, when and why.

  4. Compare the runs

    Run the season once with no launch as the control. The difference between runs is what your decision changed.

The study

Study: launching a new folding smart trainer into the UK's Black Friday and Christmas season

To show the Rider Panel working, we invented a brand called Northfold and a product, the DD1. Northfold is not a real company. The DD1 is a smart trainer: a stand that turns your own bike into an indoor exercise bike. It is quiet and accurate. It folds flat to 14cm deep for small homes.

It launches in mid-November at £499, stocked by Sigma Sports, Tredz and Halfords with strong reviews. Every rival is real, at its real UK price and Black Friday deal. Wahoo's KICKR CORE 2 drops to £399.99.

Why the same season is run three times

All 500 riders lived the same seven weeks three times, from 14 November to 31 December. That's the season that decides trainer sales. Black Friday lands in it, with Christmas spending close behind. Each time, they had the same lives and the same weather. Every rival product had the same price and the same Black Friday deal. The only thing that changed between the three runs was Northfold. So any difference in what riders bought comes from the launch decision and nothing else.

Run 1 is the control. Northfold doesn't exist, so it shows how the market behaves without the launch: who buys a trainer anyway and which brands they choose. Without it, you can't tell which Northfold sales are new buyers and which were taken from rivals.

Run 2 is the launch as planned: £499 all season, through the big retailers, with strong reviews. Comparing it with Run 1 shows what the launch itself did.

Run 3 tests a fix. In Run 2, most riders who nearly bought said price was the reason they didn't. So Run 3 makes one change, a £399 Black Friday price. Comparing Run 3 with Run 2 shows what that one decision is worth.

Then word of mouth. The riders know each other, with 1,290 ties between friends and club mates in the same towns. After each run, every rider heard what the people they know had bought and what they thought of it. Then each one could change their mind. In one season it changed little: 9 decisions out of 830, with 3 of them switching to a Northfold. Most riders held back for reasons a friend's new trainer doesn't fix, like money or a lack of space.

What this could mean in sales

What this could mean in sales: a three-step estimate

The panel's riders buy a trainer far more often than real cyclists, so we don't scale its numbers up. The estimate takes the size of the market from real data. It takes one number from the panel: how often riders choose Northfold once they've come across it.

Our best estimate is about 185,000 indoor trainers a year in the UK, worked out from market revenue, low confidence. 16% of a year's UK trainer searches fall between 14 November and 31 December, which gives about 30,000.
This one is up to your launch plan. For scale, JetBlack, an established challenger brand, gets about 14% of UK trainer brand searches. The Tacx Nēra got under 1% in its launch month.
3 Share who then choose Northfold, from the panel
Of the riders who came across Northfold and bought a trainer, this is the share who chose Northfold. The range comes from re-sampling the 500 riders 4,000 times.
Estimated Northfold DD1 sales, 14 November to 31 December

An estimate for comparing plans, not a sales forecast. The £399 Black Friday price also brought in riders who weren't going to buy a trainer at all, which this doesn't count, so it's cautious for that plan.

    Why people didn't buy

    Every rider who shortlisted Northfold and walked away told us what would have changed their mind. This is the most useful output for a brand, because it turns a sales number into a to-do list.

    Reasons are tagged from each rider's own words. A rider can give more than one reason.
